node.label: Laurence Fontaine
node.date_label: Histoire du colportage en Europe (1993; English 1996) · L’économie morale (2008; English 2014) · Le Marché (2014)
node.description: In L’économie morale (2008; translated as The Moral Economy, 2014), Laurence Fontaine argues that aristocratic and merchant cultures of credit coexisted, competed and changed one another in early modern Europe. Credit connected people across social ranks through obligations that could sustain survival while also producing dependence; the history of markets therefore cannot be reduced to a passage from social solidarity to impersonal calculation. Her research on peddlers, migration and women’s economic activity follows the practices through which people sought resources and room to act. Philippe Minard welcomed the inquiry into everyday economic life but argued in 2009 that its emphasis on coexistence understated the market’s growing dominance as an organizing principle between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Le Marché (2014) pursued the possibilities and dangers of access to exchange. Arnault Skornicki criticized its account of emancipation and power in 2015; Fontaine replied that her analysis also identified exclusion, short-termism and individualism as dangers within markets and that the Enlightenment thinkers she engaged placed political action and justice at the centre of moralizing the market. A CNRS economic and social historian, she formerly taught at the European University Institute.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Histoire du colportage en Europe (1993); History of Pedlars in Europe (English edition, 1996); “Homo creditus et construction de la confiance au XVIIIe siècle” (1997), with John Brewer; “Women’s Economic Spheres and Credit in Pre-industrial Europe” (2001); L’économie morale. Pauvreté, crédit et confiance dans l’Europe préindustrielle (2008); The Moral Economy: Poverty, Credit, and Trust in Early Modern Europe (English translation, 2014); Le Marché. Histoire et usages d’une conquête sociale (2014); “Reconsidering the Moral Economy in France at the End of the Eighteenth Century” (2019).
node.scope_note: The Moral Economy: English introduction pp. 1–7 and prologue pp. 8–10 read; French original and remaining book chapters unread. Women’s Economic Spheres: preview pages 15–22 read; remainder unread. Minard: selected review passages; Skornicki: pp. 1–2 and 6; Fontaine’s 2015 reply: pp. 7–9 complete. The 2019 chapter is abstract-only. The pedlars book, Le Marché, the Brewer coauthored chapter and other listed books are not read in full. Works cited by Fontaine are not independently read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014), Fontaine explicitly follows Marc Bloch in moving between present questions and past practices.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: English introduction p. 2: “manner of a Marc Bloch.” Explicit methodological acknowledgment; no particular Bloch title is identified and no comprehensive dependence is claimed. Full book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Bloch: dialogue between past and present

proposed_edges.relationship: In L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014), Fontaine uses Foucault to frame the diffuse power operating through credit relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: English introduction p. 5 and note 11 link diffuse social power to Sécurité, territoire, population (lectures 1977–1978; published 2004); p. 2 also invokes genealogical questioning. This is a specified analytical resource, not an assertion of wholesale adherence. Cited Foucault volume unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Explaining chapter 3 of Le Marché (2014) in her 2015 reply to Skornicki, Fontaine argues that migrant merchant networks cut across Braudel’s division between subsistence markets, small commerce and high capital.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author response, PDF p. 7, paragraph outlining chapters 1–4: “casse la tripartition braudélienne.” Specific objection to that division, not a rejection of all Braudel’s history; Le Marché and the relevant Braudel books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fontaine and John Brewer coauthored “Homo creditus et construction de la confiance au XVIIIe siècle” (1997), in La Construction sociale de la confiance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: EUI report on 1997, published 1998, printed/PDF p. 50: the chapter appears under each author and is credited “with” the other, pp. 161–176. Corrects the counted record’s Brouwers, John to John Brewer. Chapter body unread; no individual division of arguments inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Reconsidering the Moral Economy in France at the End of the Eighteenth Century” (2019), Fontaine takes up Thompson’s concept of the moral economy and, through essays of 1777 on eradicating mendicancy, places his thesis in a wider context of charity, religion, Enlightenment and aspirations to political equality (per the abstract).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Displayed EBSCO abstract, final sentence, says the essays situate Thompson’s thesis within that wider intellectual and political context. Abstract only; no claim about the chapter’s detailed conclusions or a rejection of Thompson. Publisher preview confirms title/year but does not include chapter.

proposed_edges.relationship: L’économie morale (2008; English translation 2014) explains early modern exchange through overlapping cultures of credit and the dependencies linking lenders and borrowers across social ranks.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: English introduction pp. 3–6 states the credit network and competing-cultures argument; Minard 2009, pp. 1–3, identifies its contribution to ordinary economic practices. This is a substantive contribution to economic history, not an employer or topic-only link. Later monograph chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Women’s Economic Spheres and Credit in Pre-industrial Europe” (2001), Fontaine argues that household provisioning and commerce could enlarge women’s economic room for action while legal and marital status constrained it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter preview, pp. 15–22, especially p. 19 on provisioning and pp. 20–22 on widowhood, trading capacity and restrictions. Claim retains regional and status differences; no uniform European emancipation asserted. Chapter remainder unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women’s economic action and legal constraints

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Household Strategies for Survival: An Introduction’ (2000), coauthored with Jürgen Schlumbohm, Laurence Fontaine contributes to the history of the family by treating household composition and boundaries as negotiated and by connecting family change to economic survival.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF’s methodological discussion on pp. 3–7 and its discussion of uncertainty, family relations and political economies on pp. 10–17. Pages 4–5 explicitly identify limitations of household-and-family history and propose an integrated research approach; p. 15 examines how migration changes family membership, obligations and power. The authorial footnote on p. 1 attributes pp. 10–17 to Fontaine and pp. 1–10 to Schlumbohm. The relationship preserves joint authorship, with Fontaine’s own section supplying the family-change component; it does not credit her alone with the wording on p. 5. This is a contribution evidenced by substantive argument, not merely editorial co-credit or a claim that she originated family-strategy research.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘The Circulation of Luxury Goods in Eighteenth-Century Paris: Social Redistribution and an Alternative Currency’ (2003), Laurence Fontaine contributes to consumption and material-culture history by examining ordinary and lesser-known circuits distributing luxury and fashion goods in Paris.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s abstract, bibliographic information and displayed notes. The abstract explicitly distinguishes the study’s focus on distribution from earlier emphasis on production and consumption, then identifies the ordinary circuits investigated. The claim is limited to that stated research contribution. The complete chapter was not accessible and is not represented as read; no detailed findings about redistribution, pawn credit or consumer behaviour are inferred from its title or notes. The publisher’s chapter citation and copyright give 2003; the later electronic publication is not treated as the original year. No editor–contributor relationship with Maxine Berg is inferred.
proposed_edges.map_label: Ordinary circuits of luxury and fashion
